I am fifty years old and have farmed these eight mu in Quzhou County for over thirty years. I only finished primary school, but I know this land and the weather here better than any book. This year I will stick to my winter wheat and summer maize rotation on all eight mu because it is the safest way to put food on the table and still have grain to sell. Everyone in my village does this double-crop system, and the buyers come to the village to purchase both crops. I thought about planting cotton or watermelons like some younger farmers, but my wife and I do not have the extra labor for hand-picking cotton or the stomach for such volatile prices. For wheat, I will use an improved variety I have bought from the local cooperative for years—it gives steady yields and the mill pays a fair price. For the summer maize that follows the wheat harvest in early June, I will buy hybrid seed because it out-yields traditional seed by a wide margin and the seed dealer gives me a discount for being a repeat customer. I will rotary-till the soil before sowing wheat to break up the stubble and control weeds, but for maize I will plant directly into the wheat residue with no-tillage to save diesel and time during the busy summer season. I will irrigate the wheat four times—once before winter and three times in spring—and the maize twice during its critical silking and grain-filling stages. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer as a basal dose and topdress with urea, applying about thirty-five kilograms of nitrogen per mu for wheat and twenty-two kilograms for maize, plus the usual phosphorus and potassium. I will also spray pesticides three times for each crop: once with herbicide and twice with insecticide to protect against aphids and stem borers.
